title: A Cupbearer's Prayer
sum: In Susa, the Persian winter capital, Nehemiah, a Jew in the king's service, hears from his brother Hanani that the survivors in Judah are in misery and that Jerusalem's wall lies broken and its gates burned. He sits down and weeps, and for days he mourns, fasts and prays.

His prayer, given in full, praises the God who keeps covenant, confesses Israel's sin and his own, and reminds God of his word through Moses: scattering if Israel was unfaithful, gathering if it turned back. It ends with a request for success before "this man," and only then does Nehemiah tell us who he is: the king's cupbearer.
readings: Read as a memoir

The chapter opens a first-person account unlike anything else in the Bible's histories. Nehemiah tells his own story, his own grief and his own prayer, and the reader sees events from inside the mind of a court official. Historians value the memoir as a firsthand source, while remembering that a memoir presents its writer's side.
Read as a model of prayer

Jewish and Christian readers have long taken 1:4–11 as a pattern: grief turned into fasting, praise before petition, confession that includes oneself, appeal to God's own promises, and a concrete request. The prayer is woven from Deuteronomy and Solomon's prayer (1 Kings 8), so it shows a man who prays Scripture back to God.

views.H: A true account from Nehemiah's own pen, in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes I (445 BC). The prayer was prayed over the months from Kislev to Nisan and records his real words, or their substance.
views.C: Most scholars accept the memoir as genuinely Nehemiah's, written soon after 433 BC. Some think the long prayer (1:5–11) was added or expanded by the editor, since its language is the standard Deuteronomic style of Ezra 9, Nehemiah 9 and Daniel 9; others see it as Nehemiah's own.
views.A: Susa's palace, the office of cupbearer and a Jewish official at court all fit what Persian and Greek sources show. Babylonian tablets of the Murashu firm name Jews among those doing business with Persian officials in Nehemiah's century.
views.J: Rabbinic tradition honors Nehemiah's grief for Jerusalem; mourning for Zion became part of Jewish prayer and the fast of the Ninth of Av. His confession in the plural matches the Jewish prayers of confession said on fast days and the Day of Atonement.
views.X: Christians read Nehemiah as a model of the believer in a secular workplace who prays before acting. His intercession for a people he did not personally wrong is often set beside Moses (Exodus 32:11–13), Daniel (Daniel 9) and Christ, who prays for his people (John 17).

deep.b:
Nehemiah dates his story by the reign of Artaxerxes (2:1; 5:14). The usual view is Artaxerxes I (465–424 BC), so the news came in Kislev (November–December) 446 BC and the audience with the king in Nisan (March–April) 445 BC. The best outside evidence is an Aramaic letter from the Jewish colony at Elephantine in Egypt, written in 407 BC, which mentions "the sons of Sanballat, governor of Samaria" and the high priest Johanan (12:22–23). If Sanballat's sons were active in 407, Sanballat himself fits a generation earlier, under Artaxerxes I. A few scholars have put Nehemiah under Artaxerxes II (404–359 BC), in 384 BC, but this has little support today.

The odd order, Kislev before Nisan in the same year, is explained in two main ways: Nehemiah counted regnal years from the king's accession, which came in late summer, or he used a calendar year beginning in the autumn (Tishri), as later Jewish reckoning does. A few suggest that 1:1 once read "nineteenth year." Harold Hoehner counted Artaxerxes' years from Tishri in a way that puts the news in Kislev 445 and the audience in Nisan 444 BC, which is why some books give 444. The difference matters to those who count Daniel's seventy weeks from 2:1; see the chapter 2 page.

Almost every line of 1:5–11 echoes earlier books. The address comes from Deuteronomy 7:9 and 7:21. The plea for an open ear and eyes repeats Solomon (1 Kings 8:28–29, 52). The confession uses Leviticus 26:40. The "word to Moses" sums up Leviticus 26:33 and Deuteronomy 4:25–31 and 30:1–5, the last quoted almost exactly: "Even if you have been driven to the farthest edge of the sky, the LORD your God will gather you from there" (Deuteronomy 30:4). The appeal "they are your servants and your people, whom you ransomed" recalls Moses' prayer after the golden calf (Deuteronomy 9:26–29). The prayer thus rests on two promises: Moses' promise that a scattered people who turn back will be gathered, and Solomon's prayer that God would hear exiles who pray toward his chosen place.

echoes: Deuteronomy 7:9; Deuteronomy 7:21; Deuteronomy 30:1–5; Deuteronomy 9:26–29; Leviticus 26:33–45; 1 Kings 8:28–30; 1 Kings 8:46–53; Daniel 9:4–19; Ezra 9:6–15; 9:6–37; Ezra 4:7–23; Genesis 40:1

settings.by: Hanani, Nehemiah's brother, and men from Judah
settings.to: Nehemiah, at the Persian court in Susa
settings.when: Kislev (November–December) of the twentieth year of Artaxerxes, 446 BC (445 on Hoehner's count)
settings.why: To tell a Jew in high office how things stood in Judah, perhaps hoping he could help. Knowing that the visitors came to a man near the king explains why their report turns at once into a plan.
settings.readers: For the book's first readers in Persian or early Greek Judah, the scene showed that the walled city they lived in began with prayer and with God's hand on a faithful servant at a foreign court.

settings.what: Nehemiah's prayer of confession and request
settings.to: God, "the LORD, God of the heavens"; prayed in Susa, far from Jerusalem
settings.when: In the month of Kislev at Susa, and on through the months until Nisan ("day and night," 1:6), after the news of Jerusalem's broken walls
settings.why: To confess the people's sin, to remind God of his own promise through Moses to gather a scattered people who turn back, and to ask for success when Nehemiah speaks to the king. Because it is addressed to God by a man who must face the king, the prayer ends with a plea about "this man": the real power is God's.
settings.readers: For later readers in Judah, the prayer modeled how a people under foreign rule could pray: confessing, trusting God's promises, and expecting him to move the hearts of kings.
views: Traditional and many modern readers: Nehemiah's own words, or their substance, written into his memoir.
Some critical scholars: Nehemiah prayed, but the prayer as written was shaped in the standard style of Persian-period confessions (Ezra 9; Nehemiah 9; Daniel 9).

title: Leave from the King
sum: Four months later, as Nehemiah serves wine, the king notices his sad face. Nehemiah, afraid, explains that the city of his ancestors' graves lies in ruins. When the king asks what he wants, he prays silently, then asks to be sent to rebuild it, with letters for safe passage and for timber. The king, with the queen beside him, grants it all, and Nehemiah credits "my God's good hand."

With an armed escort he reaches Jerusalem, to the displeasure of Sanballat and Tobiah. After three days he inspects the walls secretly by night, then calls the leaders to rebuild so that the city will no longer be a disgrace. They agree. When Sanballat, Tobiah and Geshem mock and hint at rebellion, Nehemiah answers that the God of the heavens will give success, and that they have no share in Jerusalem.
readings: Read as court history

The audience scene is full of court detail: the wine service, the danger of a sad face, the queen's presence, the safe-conduct letters and the royal park. Persian documents, such as the Arsames letters authorizing rations for a traveling official, show this was how the empire worked.
Read as providence

No miracle happens. Nehemiah prays, chooses his moment and speaks carefully, and the king says yes. The memoir's verdict, "my God's good hand was on me," is the key to the whole book: God works through ordinary means, including a foreign king's mood at dinner.

views.H: A historical audience in Nisan 445 BC, followed by Nehemiah's journey and inspection. The king's permission was given in letters (2:7–9).
views.C: Accepted as part of the genuine memoir. Scholars note the dramatic shaping: the king's three questions, Nehemiah's fear and the secret night ride build suspense. Some think Nehemiah held more official authority from the start than the scene suggests.
views.A: Royal letters for travelers, royal parks (paradeisoi) with keepers, and garrisons near temples are all known from the Persian empire. The new governor's arrival with soldiers would have signaled to Samaria and Ammon that Jerusalem now had the king's backing.
views.J: In Jewish memory Nehemiah is above all Jerusalem's rebuilder: Ben Sira praises him as the one "who lifted our fallen walls back up" (Sirach 49:13). Many commentators note that before a foreign king he spoke of "the city of my ancestors' graves" rather than naming Jerusalem.
views.X: Many Christians count Daniel's seventy weeks from this verse (Daniel 9:25), so 2:1–8 has a special place in Christian prophecy. Christian readers also hold up Nehemiah's quick prayer before speaking (2:4) as a model.

deep.b:
Daniel 9:25 speaks of seventy "sevens" (490 years) beginning a span "from the time a word goes out to bring back and build Jerusalem, until an anointed ruler" (freshly translated). Nehemiah 2 is one of several candidates for that "word." Readers count very differently:

From Artaxerxes' twentieth year (Nehemiah 2:1–8). Julius Africanus, about AD 220, first counted from this year, and Eusebius preserved his reckoning. Robert Anderson (1881) counted 69 weeks of "prophetic years" of 360 days from Nisan 445 BC to Palm Sunday, AD 32. Harold Hoehner (1977) counted from Nisan 444 BC to Christ's entry into Jerusalem in AD 33. Many dispensational readers follow this view and place the seventieth week in the future.

From Artaxerxes' seventh year (Ezra 7, 458/457 BC). Others count 483 ordinary years from Ezra's commission to about AD 27, the start of Jesus' ministry, with the cutting off of the anointed one in the middle of the seventieth week. Isaac Newton offered a version of this count, and Seventh-day Adventists are its best-known modern users. Its supporters note that Ezra 7 contains a royal decree; Nehemiah 2 contains only letters.

From Cyrus (538 BC). Others start with Cyrus. His decree (Ezra 1:1–4) concerns the Temple, but Isaiah says Cyrus will also rebuild the city (Isaiah 44:28; Isaiah 45:13). Many of these readers, such as E. J. Young and Meredith Kline, take the numbers as symbolic, a sabbath of sabbaths leading to the Messiah's work, rather than as exact arithmetic. Jerome's commentary on Daniel already listed several competing counts and declined to choose.

The critical view. Most critical scholars date Daniel 9 to about 165 BC and read the "word" as Jeremiah's prophecy of rebuilding (Jeremiah 25:11–12; Jeremiah 29:10). The 490 years run, schematically, from the fall of Jerusalem to the crisis under Antiochus IV, and the anointed one "cut off" is the high priest Onias III, murdered in 171 BC. On this view Nehemiah 2 is not in view at all.

The Jewish view. The rabbinic chronology Seder Olam Rabbah and Rashi count the 490 years from the destruction of the First Temple to the destruction of the Second (AD 70): seventy years of exile and 420 years of the Second Temple. On ordinary dates, 586 BC to AD 70 is 656 years; the count works on the rabbinic chronology, which gives the Persian period only 34 years (Seder Olam 30) and so puts the First Temple's fall about 423 BC. The first "anointed" is Cyrus, whom Isaiah calls the LORD's anointed (Isaiah 45:1), and Rashi takes the anointed one "cut off" (Daniel 9:26) as King Agrippa, the last king before the Second Temple fell.

Nehemiah itself never mentions Daniel or a prophecy of years. The only date it gives is the twentieth year of Artaxerxes; it is usually dated to 445 BC, or to 444 BC on Hoehner's count, as the chapter 1 page explains.

deep.h: The night ride and the city
deep.b: Nehemiah's inspection covers only the southern part of the city, from the Valley Gate on the west, around the south end at the Dung Gate, and up the Kidron valley on the east, where fallen stone blocked his animal. Archaeologists agree that Persian-period Jerusalem was small, mainly the eastern ridge (the City of David) and the Temple mount. Eilat Mazar identified a stretch of wall and a tower above the Gihon spring as Nehemiah's work; Israel Finkelstein and others date the same remains earlier or later and argue that the Persian city was tiny and that Nehemiah's wall has not been found with certainty. The debate affects how we picture the fifty-two days (6:15), not the story's main points.

echoes: Ezra 4:7–23; Ezra 7:6; Ezra 7:9; Ezra 7:27–28; Ezra 8:22; Proverbs 21:1; Daniel 9:25; Isaiah 44:28; Isaiah 45:13; Esther 4:11; Esther 5:1–3; Genesis 41:14–16

settings.by: Nehemiah, and King Artaxerxes in dialogue
settings.to: King Artaxerxes I, with the queen sitting beside him, probably at a private meal
settings.when: Nisan (March–April) 445 BC (444 on Hoehner's count), in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes, four months after the news of 1:3
settings.why: To win the king's leave to rebuild Jerusalem without naming it as the city the king had recently ordered stopped (Ezra 4:21). Knowing the danger, a cupbearer with a sad face before an absolute king, explains Nehemiah's fear, his silent prayer and his careful words about family graves.
settings.readers: For later readers it was the founding charter of the walled city: the king had approved it, and God's good hand had moved the king.

settings.to: The Jews of Jerusalem, its priests, nobles and deputies, and the others who would do the work
settings.when: After his secret night inspection, a few days after his arrival in Jerusalem in 445 (or 444) BC
settings.why: To persuade the local leaders, who had seen earlier attempts fail (Ezra 4:23), that rebuilding was possible now: God's hand and the king's words were both behind him. He speaks of "we" and of shared disgrace, making the project theirs.
settings.readers: For the book's first readers, living inside the rebuilt wall, the scene showed that it began when a governor shared the shame of the ruins with the people of Jerusalem and they chose to build.

settings.what: The taunt and the charge of rebellion
settings.by: Sanballat the Horonite, Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite, and Geshem the Arab
settings.to: Nehemiah and the Jewish builders
settings.when: As the work begins, 445 (or 444) BC
settings.why: To mock the builders and to threaten them with the one charge that had stopped the walls before: rebellion against the king (Ezra 4:12–16). The words were meant to frighten the Jews and perhaps to gather evidence for a report to Persia.
views: The memoir's own view, followed by most traditional readers.
Many historians: established neighboring rulers alarmed by a strong Jerusalem under a governor with royal backing.

settings.to: Sanballat, Tobiah and Geshem
settings.when: In reply to their taunt, as the work begins
settings.why: To refuse the charge without arguing politics, and to deny the opponents any share, legal right or memorial in Jerusalem. The answer draws a boundary around the community, the same boundary claimed in Ezra 4:3.
settings.readers: For later readers it defined who had a part in Jerusalem, a live question in the late Persian period, when Samaria built its own temple on Mount Gerizim.

traditions.q: Does the count of Daniel's seventy weeks (Daniel 9:24–27) start with Artaxerxes' letters to Nehemiah (Nehemiah 2:1–8), and how does it end?
views: Many count 69 weeks of 360-day years from Nehemiah 2 to Jesus' entry into Jerusalem (Robert Anderson, 1881; Harold Hoehner, 1977). Then the clock stops: the seventieth week is still to come, as a seven-year tribulation after the church is taken up.

Most Reformed teachers see all seventy weeks fulfilled in Christ, with no gap: he came, was cut off, and ended the sacrifices by his death. Many, such as E. J. Young and Meredith Kline, read the numbers as a pattern rather than exact years, and some start the count from Cyrus.

The count starts with Artaxerxes' decree for Ezra in 457 BC (Ezra 7), reaches Jesus' baptism in AD 27 and his death in AD 31, and also begins the 2,300 days of Daniel 8:14. Those end in 1844, when Christ began the last phase of his work in the heavenly sanctuary (Fundamental Beliefs 24).

The church fathers read the weeks as a prophecy of Christ but counted them in many ways, as Jerome showed, and the Church has never fixed a count. Many Catholic scholars today read Daniel 9 as written in the time of Antiochus IV.

title: Everyone at the Wall
sum: The chapter lists who rebuilt each part of the wall, beginning with the high priest Eliashib at the Sheep Gate and going counterclockwise around the city back to the Sheep Gate. Priests, Levites, temple servants, goldsmiths, perfume makers, traders, district officials and townspeople from Jericho, Tekoa, Gibeon, Mizpah, Zanoah, Beth-zur and Keilah each take a section or a gate.

Some repair the stretch in front of their own houses. Shallum works with his daughters, the men of Tekoa do two sections though their nobles refuse, and Baruch works with special zeal. The list is the best source we have for the layout of Persian-period Jerusalem, and its many names show a whole people at work.
readings: Read as a building record

The list reads like an official record, perhaps from the governor's archive, naming the gates, towers and sections and who was responsible for each. It is written in the third person, unlike the memoir around it, which suggests Nehemiah or his editor took it from a document.
Read as a portrait of the community

The chapter honors ordinary people. Rulers and craftsmen, men and women, priests and traders appear side by side, each named. Tamara Eskenazi and others see here the book's main idea: the restoration was the work of the whole people of God, not of a few heroes.

views.H: A true record of the builders, preserved by Nehemiah. The order follows the wall around the city.
views.C: Probably an older document, perhaps from the Temple archive, inserted into the memoir. Some think it describes the work as finished (the dedication of 3:1, the doors set in place) and so may have been written later than chapter 4, which still shows the gaps open.
views.A: The districts (pelekh) and their officials fit Persian provincial administration. The gates, the Pool of Shelah, the steps from the City of David and the Ophel can be partly located; the Broad Wall of 3:8 was found in the Jewish Quarter in 1970.
views.J: Jewish tradition sees in the list the same love for Jerusalem that runs through Psalm 122 and 137. The Masoretes marked 3:32 as the midpoint of Ezra–Nehemiah.
views.X: Christian preachers have often used the chapter as a picture of the church: each member with a part (1 Corinthians 12), some working near home, some far away, and every name remembered (Hebrews 6:10).

deep.b: The list moves counterclockwise. In the north, where there was no valley to protect the city, are the Sheep Gate, the towers of the Hundred and of Hananel, the Fish Gate and the Jeshanah Gate (3:1–6). On the west run the Broad Wall, the Tower of the Ovens and the Valley Gate (3:7–13). At the south are the Dung Gate, the Spring Gate, the Pool of Shelah and the steps of the City of David (3:14–15). The east side, above the Kidron, has the longest list of small sections: David's tombs, the pool, the Warriors' House, the armory, the bend in the wall, the high priest's house, the Ophel, the Water Gate, the Horse Gate, the East Gate and the Miphkad Gate (3:16–31), before the list returns to the Sheep Gate (3:32). Many sections on the east are short and tied to houses, which suggests the wall there ran along the top of the slope, higher than the old line of the monarchy, which had collapsed into the Kidron.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the list as a roll of honor
deep.b: My own suggestion: the list of builders works the way the "remember" prayers do for Nehemiah himself (5:19; 13:31). It sets each builder's name before God and the community, a roll of honor and also a roll of shame, since it records that the nobles of Tekoa would not bend their necks (3:5). The same people later appear in the pledge of chapter 10 and in the troubles of chapter 13 (Meshullam son of Berechiah, 3:4 and 6:18; Eliashib, 3:1 and 13:4). A first reader would see who had built and who had held back, and might judge later failures in that light. Scholars have long noted that the list honors the community (Eskenazi) and that it is a separate document (Williamson), and "honor roll" readings are common in commentaries and preaching. Ursula Haasbroek's study of the builders' names (University of Pretoria, 2023) also reads the names as meaningful rather than merely descriptive. My own addition is the link to the "remember" prayers: the list as a record set before God that sets up the later judgments of chapters 6 and 13.

echoes: Jeremiah 31:38–40; Zechariah 14:10; 2 Chronicles 26:9; 2 Chronicles 32:5; 2 Chronicles 33:14; 12:31–40; John 5:2; John 9:7; Ezra 2:35

settings.what: The list of the builders of the wall
settings.by: An official record, probably kept by Nehemiah's administration or the Temple, and set into the memoir
settings.to: The community of Judah and Jerusalem, and before them God; the list names those who took part
settings.when: Written during or after the rebuilding of 445 (or 444) BC; some think after the work was finished, since it records doors in place
settings.why: To record who built each section and gate, and so to honor them and fix responsibility. Knowing it is a record explains its repetitive form and its care with names and places. It also answers the opponents' sneer (4:2): the whole people, not a few, rebuilt the wall.
settings.readers: For later readers it was a family record of honor: their ancestors' names stood in the account of Jerusalem's rebuilding, as other families' names stood in the returnees' list (7:6–73).
views: Some scholars: Nehemiah drew it up himself.
Most scholars: an archival list, in a different style, inserted into the memoir.

title: Sword and Trowel
sum: Sanballat mocks the "worn-out Jews" before the army of Samaria, and Tobiah jokes that a fox could knock down their wall. Nehemiah answers with a prayer for judgment, and the people build on until the wall is joined all around at half its height, "for the people's heart was in the work." Then Sanballat, Tobiah, the Arabs, the Ammonites and the Ashdodites plot an attack, while in Judah the workers sing that their strength is failing.

Nehemiah prays, posts guards, arms the people by families and tells them to remember the great and fearsome Lord and fight for their homes. When the plot is exposed, work resumes, but now half his men stand armed while half build, every builder wears a sword, and a trumpeter stands by Nehemiah to sound the alarm. Workers stay in the city at night, and no one takes off his clothes.
readings: Read as a story of courage

The chapter moves from mockery to threat to readiness. Each time the enemy acts, Nehemiah prays and acts: prayer and guard (4:9), courage speech (4:14), work with weapons (4:16–23). The story has inspired many communities building under threat.
Read with the opponents in view

Historians note that we hear only Nehemiah's side. Sanballat, Tobiah and their allies were the established leaders of the neighboring provinces, and a walled Jerusalem under a new governor changed the balance of power. Their mockery and plots were real, but so were their interests. The topic page sets out both readings.

views.H: A true account of real threats. The enemies' plans were stopped because God frustrated them (4:15) and because Nehemiah organized the defense.
views.C: Part of the memoir, with its strong first-person view. Scholars note that no actual attack is recorded; the threat itself was the weapon. The prayer of 4:4–5 and the lament of 4:10 may preserve traditional poetic forms.
views.A: Persian governors could not easily make war on each other without the king's leave, so the opponents' tools were mockery, rumor and threats rather than open war. Ashdod was a Persian province on the coast; the Arabs of Qedar controlled the south.
views.J: The image of builders holding a weapon in one hand has had a long life in Jewish memory, and in modern Israel has been applied to those who built and guarded at the same time. Compare the later rabbinic rule that one does not rely on a miracle (Bavli Pesachim 64b).
views.X: Christians have read the chapter as a picture of the life of faith: work and watchfulness, prayer and action. "We prayed to our God, and ... kept watchmen posted" (4:9) is a classic text on trusting God while using means.

deep.b:
The memoir's view, which most Jewish and Christian readers have followed, is that Sanballat, Tobiah and Geshem were enemies of God's work, and that their mockery and plots showed hostility to the LORD's city. Nehemiah prays that God will not forgive them (4:5).

Many historians add another view. Sanballat was the governor of Samaria, a larger and richer province; his sons bore names honoring the LORD, and the Jews of Elephantine later appealed to his sons for help with their temple. Tobiah, also a worshiper of the LORD by name, was married into a leading Jerusalem family and had friends among Judah's nobles (6:17–19). Geshem's Arabs controlled the trade routes. To them, a new governor with royal backing who walled the city and shut them out ("you have no share in Jerusalem," 2:20) was a political threat. The conflict was about worship and identity, but also about power, trade and land.

Both views can be held together: Nehemiah's opponents had real interests, and from the book's point of view those interests set them against what God was doing. Readers should remember that the memoir gives only one side.

Nehemiah's prayer in 4:4–5 asks God to return the enemies' scorn on their own heads and not to forgive their sin. It echoes Jeremiah's prayer against his persecutors (Jeremiah 18:23) and psalms of lament (Psalm 79:12; Psalm 123:3–4). Readers have responded in three ways. Some defend it: it leaves vengeance to God rather than taking it (Romans 12:19), and mocking the builders was mocking God. Some find it hard to square with Jesus' command to pray for enemies (Matthew 5:44). Many see it as an honest prayer of people under threat, recorded rather than recommended.

echoes: Ezra 4:1–24; Jeremiah 18:23; Psalm 79:12; Psalm 123:3–4; Lamentations 5:18; Deuteronomy 7:21; Deuteronomy 20:1–4; Exodus 14:14; Matthew 26:41; Ephesians 6:10–18

settings.what: The taunts of Sanballat and Tobiah
settings.by: Sanballat, governor of Samaria, and Tobiah the Ammonite at his side
settings.to: Sanballat's "brothers" (his officials or kinsmen) and the army of Samaria; the words were meant to reach the Jews too
settings.when: When Sanballat heard that the wall was being built, in the summer of 445 (or 444) BC
settings.why: To ridicule the builders before Samaria's troops, to stiffen his own side and to discourage the Jews when the mockery reached them. The questions mock every hope: restoring the city, sacrificing, finishing quickly, reusing burned stones.
views: Many historians: a rival governor's public show of strength against a new neighbor.

settings.by: Nehemiah, speaking for the builders ("our God")
settings.to: God
settings.when: At once, on hearing the taunts
settings.why: To hand the insult over to God and ask for judgment, rather than answering the enemies directly. Because it is said to God, not to Sanballat, the prayer turns anger into an appeal to the divine judge.
settings.readers: For later readers under the contempt of neighbors, it gave words for a community's anger before God.

settings.by: The people of Judah, the workers carrying rubble
settings.to: Themselves and their leaders; perhaps a work song
settings.when: When the wall had reached half its height and the enemies were plotting
settings.why: To voice exhaustion: the porters were failing and the rubble seemed endless. Its rhythm may be that of a lament or work song, sung as they carried loads.

settings.what: The enemies' threat and the villagers' warning
settings.by: The enemies (4:11), and the Jews living near them (4:12)
settings.to: The Jews in Jerusalem, especially the builders
settings.when: As the plot formed
settings.why: The enemies' words were meant to spread fear of a surprise attack. The villagers' repeated warning, perhaps with a plea for their men to come home, shows how the threat pulled workers away from the wall.

settings.to: The nobles, the deputies and the rest of the people, armed by families behind the wall
settings.when: After the plot became known and guards were posted
settings.why: To steady frightened people with the words of Israel's holy wars (Deuteronomy 7:21; Deuteronomy 20:3–4) and to remind them that they were fighting for their families and homes.

settings.to: The nobles, the deputies and the rest of the people, spread along the wall
settings.when: When work resumed with half the men armed
settings.why: To set up a system of defense along a long wall: gather where the ram's horn sounds. The closing "Our God will fight for us" turns an order into a promise.

settings.what: The order to stay in the city
settings.to: The workers, including those from towns outside Jerusalem, and their servants
settings.when: During the rest of the building
settings.why: To keep a night guard in the city and keep workers from going home each evening. It shows the cost to families from the villages.

title: The Outcry of the Poor
sum: A great cry rises from the common people and their wives, not against foreign enemies but against fellow Jews. Families need grain; farmers have mortgaged fields, vineyards and houses in a famine; others have borrowed to pay the king's tax; and some have already handed over their daughters as slaves, with no power to redeem them.

Nehemiah is furious. He confronts the nobles and deputies, calls a great assembly, and shames them: while Jews abroad buy back their brothers from foreigners, they are selling their brothers. He calls for the loans on pledge to stop and the land and interest to be returned at once. The lenders agree, swear before the priests, and Nehemiah shakes out his robe as a curse on any who break the oath. He then describes his own twelve years as governor, when he took no governor's allowance and fed 150 at his table, and prays, "My God, remember me for good."
readings: Read as social history

The chapter is a rare window on the economy of Persian Judah: famine, imperial taxes paid in silver, mortgages, interest and debt slavery. The same pattern appears across the ancient Near East, and many historians see the crisis as the result of taxation, drought and an elite that profited from both.
Read as covenant justice

The chapter applies the laws of Leviticus 25 and Deuteronomy 15 to a real crisis. The poor appeal to kinship ("our flesh is like our brothers' flesh"), Nehemiah to the fear of God, and the solution is a release of debts and land like the law's seventh year and Jubilee. Justice among God's people is part of rebuilding the city.

views.H: The events happened during or soon after the wall-building. The cry came because men were away from their fields and a famine struck.
views.C: Many scholars think 5:1–13 took place later in Nehemiah's twelve years and was placed here by theme; 5:14–19 looks back over the whole term. The chapter gives a firsthand picture of social conflict and of a governor's self-presentation.
views.A: Persian taxes in silver, recorded in Herodotus and in Babylonian archives, forced farmers to borrow. Contracts from the Murashu archive at Nippur show land pledged for loans and lost to creditors in the same century.
views.J: Jewish law on interest and on the seventh-year release rests on the Torah (Leviticus 25:35–37; Deuteronomy 15:1–11), and Nehemiah 5 reads as an early case of applying it; compare the later prozbul of Hillel (Mishnah Shevi'it 10:3), which let loans survive the seventh year so that lenders would keep lending. The Talmud faults Nehemiah's self-praise and his words against the governors before him (5:15; 5:19; Bavli Sanhedrin 93b).
views.X: Christians have read the chapter as a call to economic justice within the church, setting it beside Acts 4:32–35 and James 5:1–6. Its leader who gives up his rights for the people's sake has been compared with Paul (1 Corinthians 9:12–18).

deep.b:
The poor in 5:1–5 describe exactly what the law of Moses was meant to prevent. Leviticus 25 commands: "If your brother becomes poor and his hand slips while he is with you, hold him up" (Leviticus 25:35); "Do not take interest or profit from him. Fear your God" (Leviticus 25:36); and if he sells himself, "do not make him work the work of a slave" (Leviticus 25:39), because "they are my servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt. They must not be sold the way a slave is sold" (Leviticus 25:42). The land, too, was to return to its families in the Jubilee (Leviticus 25:10, 23–28).

Deuteronomy 15 adds a release every seventh year: "Every lender is to let go of the loan he made to his neighbor. He must not press his neighbor, his brother, for payment" (Deuteronomy 15:2), and it warns against refusing loans as the release year nears (Deuteronomy 15:9). Hebrew debt slaves go free in the seventh year, "do not send him away with empty hands" (Deuteronomy 15:13). Deuteronomy also bans interest to a brother (Deuteronomy 23:19–20) and limits pledges (Deuteronomy 24:10–13).

Nehemiah does not quote these laws, but his words carry them: "each of you against his own brother" (5:7), "the fear of our God" (5:9; Leviticus 25:36), buying back brothers (5:8; Leviticus 25:48). His reform goes beyond the letter, since he orders the return of land and interest at once, not at a set year. The people later pledge to keep the seventh-year release (10:31).

The chapter ends with Nehemiah's own account of his generosity and a prayer that God remember it (5:14–19). Readers have judged him in very different ways. Ben Sira praises him without reservation: he is "Long remembered", the one "who lifted our fallen walls back up" (Sirach 49:13). The Talmud says the book was not named for him because he took credit to himself and spoke badly of the governors before him (Bavli Sanhedrin 93b). Modern scholars differ: David Clines reads the memoir as a skilled self-defense whose claims should be weighed, not simply believed; Jacob Wright traces how it was expanded by later writers; others see a sincere leader who used his own wealth for the common good. His later actions, beating and cursing men who married foreign women (13:25), have also led many to call him harsh, while others see the firmness a fragile community needed. The site presents each reading on the topic page.

echoes: Leviticus 25:35–55; Deuteronomy 15:1–18; Deuteronomy 23:19–20; Deuteronomy 24:10–13; Exodus 21:2–11; Exodus 22:25–27; Jeremiah 34:8–22; Amos 2:6–8; 10:31; Acts 4:32–35; 1 Corinthians 9:12–18; James 5:1–6

settings.by: The common people and their wives
settings.to: Nehemiah as governor, and through him, the nobles and deputies who were their creditors; the cry is also the cry the law says God hears (Exodus 22:27)
settings.when: During or soon after the building of the wall, in a time of famine; possibly later in Nehemiah's twelve-year term
settings.why: To force a hearing for families losing land and children to debt. By naming their creditors as "our brothers" and appealing to shared flesh, they appeal to the law's protection of a poor brother.
settings.readers: For later readers, it showed that rebuilding Jerusalem's walls meant nothing if Jews were enslaving Jews inside them.

settings.what: Nehemiah's charge to the nobles and deputies
settings.to: First the nobles and deputies in private, then a great assembly of the people called against them
settings.when: After hearing the outcry, in the middle of the building years
settings.why: To shame the lenders publicly, to remind them of the fear of God and of their duty to redeem, not sell, their brothers, and to demand that pledges and interest be returned that very day. Spoken before the assembly, the words leave the creditors no room to refuse.
settings.readers: For later readers it applied the laws of Leviticus 25 and Deuteronomy 15 to their own economy.

settings.what: The oath and the acted curse
settings.by: Nehemiah, with the priests administering the oath; the assembly answers "Amen"
settings.to: The nobles and deputies who agreed to return the land and interest
settings.when: At the end of the assembly
settings.why: To make the promise binding before God: the priests' oath and the shaking of the robe called down God's curse on anyone who broke it, as Jeremiah 34 warns of a release broken.

settings.what: Nehemiah's account of his governorship and his prayer
settings.to: God ("My God, remember me for good"), and any reader of the memoir
settings.when: Written after his term ended in the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes, 433 BC, looking back over twelve years
settings.why: To set his record before God and readers: he took no governor's allowance, bought no land, fed many at his own cost, because the people's burden was heavy. The closing prayer shows the memoir's purpose: Nehemiah asks God, not people, to judge his work.
views: Many readers: an honest plea that God remember his service.
Mowinckel and von Rad: like donors' and memorial inscriptions, the memoir was written to be set before God.
Kellermann, Clines and others: an accused man's defense against critics in Judah or at court, so its claims must be weighed.

title: Plots Against the Builder
sum: With the wall complete except for the gate doors, the opponents turn their attacks on Nehemiah himself. Four times Sanballat and Geshem invite him to a meeting in the plain of Ono, and four times he replies that he is doing a great work and cannot come down. The fifth time Sanballat sends an open letter: rumor says Nehemiah is building to rebel and has prophets proclaiming him king. Nehemiah denies it and prays for strength.

Then Shemaiah, a prophet, urges him to hide in the Temple's sanctuary from assassins. Nehemiah refuses, realizing that Shemaiah was hired by Tobiah and Sanballat to make him sin. He prays God to remember them and the prophetess Noadiah. The wall is finished on the twenty-fifth of Elul, in fifty-two days, and the surrounding nations lose heart, knowing God has done it. Yet Tobiah keeps up letters with the nobles of Judah, many of whom are bound to him by oath and marriage.
readings: Read as political intrigue

Invitation, rumor, open letter, hired prophet, inside informants: the chapter is a study in political pressure. Each attack tries a different weakness: fear for his life, fear of the king, fear for his reputation.
Read as a test of discernment

Nehemiah has to judge a prophet's word. He tests it against God's law: God would not tell a layman to hide in the sanctuary. The chapter teaches that a message is not from God if it calls for sin, however spiritual it sounds.

views.H: Real plots against a real governor. The wall was finished on 25 Elul 445 BC, in fifty-two days.
views.C: Part of the memoir, which presents Nehemiah's integrity and his enemies' bad faith. The date and the fifty-two days are widely accepted; Josephus's two years and four months (Antiquities 11.179) probably counts more of the work.
views.A: An open letter accusing a governor of seeking kingship was a dangerous weapon in a Persian empire that had just put down a revolt in Egypt. The Tell el-Maskhuta bowl names Geshem's son as king of Qedar.
views.J: Nehemiah's refusal to enter the sanctuary can be compared with the law that an outsider who comes near is to be put to death (Numbers 18:7). His dismissal of a false prophecy fits Deuteronomy's rule that a prophet who leads astray is not to be heeded.
views.X: Christians often read 6:3 as a model of focus on God's calling, and the Shemaiah episode as a warning to test the spirits (1 John 4:1).

deep.b: Shemaiah's advice was a trap with two sides. If Nehemiah ran and hid, he would look like a coward and lose the people's trust. If he went into the hekhal, the sanctuary, he would break the law that only priests may enter (Numbers 18:7), a sin like King Uzziah's (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). Either way his enemies would have "something to ruin my good name with" (6:13). Nehemiah's answer, "Is a man like me going to run?", refuses both. Some readers add that if Nehemiah was a eunuch, he could not even enter the Temple courts (Deuteronomy 23:1); this is possible but uncertain (see the notes on 1:11 and 6:11).

Chapter 6 mentions several kinds of prophets: those Sanballat says Nehemiah has appointed to proclaim him king (6:7), Shemaiah the hired prophet (6:10–13), Noadiah the prophetess and "the other prophets" who tried to frighten him (6:14). Prophecy was alive in Persian Judah; Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi belong to the same era. Some scholars think these prophets hoped for a restored Davidic king, as Haggai and Zechariah had once hoped of Zerubbabel (Haggai 2:21–23; Zechariah 6:12–13), and saw Nehemiah, the Persian king's man, as an obstacle. Others think they were simply paid by Nehemiah's enemies. The text gives only his view.

echoes: Numbers 18:7; 2 Chronicles 26:16–21; Deuteronomy 13:1–5; Deuteronomy 18:20–22; Jeremiah 23:16–22; Micah 3:5–11; Haggai 2:21–23; Zechariah 6:12–13; Ezra 4:12–16; 13:4–9; 13:28; 1 John 4:1

settings.to: Nehemiah
settings.when: After the wall was closed but before the doors were hung, late summer 445 (or 444) BC
settings.why: Presented as an invitation to talks, it was meant, Nehemiah says, to lure him far from Jerusalem and harm him. Ono lay in border land near Lod, a day's journey away.

settings.to: Sanballat and Geshem
settings.when: Sent four times in answer to four invitations
settings.why: To refuse without insult: his work is too great to leave. The reply keeps him in Jerusalem and gives his enemies nothing to report.

settings.by: Sanballat, governor of Samaria, through his servant
settings.to: Nehemiah, but written open so that others along the way could read it
settings.when: The fifth message, as the wall neared completion in 445 (or 444) BC
settings.why: To accuse Nehemiah of planning revolt and of having prophets proclaim him king, and to threaten to tell the Persian king. The open letter spread the rumor whatever Nehemiah answered; its closing offer of "plans together" was a demand to submit.
views: The memoir's view: pure invention to frighten him.
Some historians: hopes for a Davidic king were alive (Haggai 2:23), which made the accusation dangerous.

settings.to: Sanballat
settings.when: In reply to the open letter
settings.why: To deny the charge flatly and name it as invention, without asking for a meeting.

settings.to: God (in the Hebrew, a short plea; in the Greek, a statement that he strengthened himself)
settings.when: In the middle of the campaign of fear
settings.why: To ask for strength against the enemies' hope that the builders' hands would go limp.

settings.by: Shemaiah son of Delaiah, son of Mehetabel, a prophet hired by Tobiah and Sanballat
settings.to: Nehemiah, who had come to his house
settings.when: Near the end of the building, while Shemaiah was "shut away indoors"
settings.why: Spoken as a prophetic warning of assassins, it was meant to frighten Nehemiah into a sin, entering the sanctuary as a layman, so that his enemies could discredit him. Knowing who paid for it turns a seemingly caring oracle into a trap.

settings.to: Shemaiah
settings.when: At once
settings.why: To refuse both to run and to break the law of the sanctuary.

settings.to: God
settings.when: After uncovering the plot
settings.why: To hand Tobiah, Sanballat, Noadiah and the other prophets over to God's judgment, the reverse of his own "remember me for good."
settings.readers: For later readers it set the enemies' names before God as a warning, just as the builders' names stood as an honor.

settings.what: The letters between Judah's nobles and Tobiah
settings.to: Each other; Tobiah's letters were also aimed at Nehemiah
settings.when: During the building, and after
settings.why: To keep up an alliance of marriage and oath, to praise Tobiah before Nehemiah and report Nehemiah's words to him, and to frighten Nehemiah. The letters show that the opposition had friends inside Jerusalem.

title: A City Guarded, a People Counted
sum: With the wall and its doors complete, Nehemiah appoints gatekeepers, singers and Levites, puts his brother Hanani and Hananiah, the trustworthy commander of the fortress, in charge of Jerusalem, and orders that the gates stay shut until the sun is high and that the citizens keep watch. But the city is large and nearly empty.

God puts it in Nehemiah's heart to enroll the people by families, and he finds the register of those who first came back from exile. The rest of the chapter copies that register: leaders, families, towns, priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, temple servants, families without proof of descent, the total of 42,360, their slaves and animals, and the gifts for the work. It is nearly the same list as Ezra 2. It ends as the seventh month arrives, leading into the reading of the law in chapter 8.
readings: Read as a document
The register is an older list, copied into the memoir as Nehemiah found it. Its differences from Ezra 2, in names and numbers, show two copies of one document, each copied by hand many times.
Read as a bridge

The list turns the book from building walls to building a people. Who belongs in the city? The answer is the families of the return, priests and Levites, and those willing to stand in the line of the first exiles. It leads straight into Ezra's reading of the law (8) and the resettlement of Jerusalem (11).

views.H: Nehemiah found and copied the list of the first return; its differences from Ezra 2 come from copying.
views.C: Scholars debate which book borrowed from which. Williamson argues that Ezra 2 was taken from here, because the list's ending (7:73) leads naturally into Nehemiah 8; others argue the reverse. Many think the register is a composite of several returns or a census of Persian Yehud.
views.A: Persian provinces kept lists of subjects for taxes and labor; the Persian title Tirshatha (7:65, 7:70) and the gold drachmas or darics (7:70–72) fit that world.
views.J: Jewish tradition treated the genealogies of the return as the basis for later rules of descent; the Mishnah lists the ten classes of descent who came up from Babylon (Mishnah Kiddushin 4:1).
views.X: Christian readers see a God who knows his people by name. Jesus' genealogies run through Zerubbabel, named first in this list (Matthew 1:12–13; Luke 3:27).

deep.h: Nehemiah 7 and Ezra 2 side by side
deep.b:
Where the Hebrew of the two lists is the same, this site's Plain uses the same English as Ezra 2; where it differs, the English differs too. The main differences, also tabled on the Ezra 2 page:

Most differences look like copying slips, especially in numbers. Neither list adds up to its total. On the borrowing question, see the note on 7:5 and the note on Ezra 2:70.

The list fills more than half of the chapter, and readers have asked why the book repeats it. In the story, Nehemiah needs it: to repopulate Jerusalem he must know which families belong to the community and where they live, and the first register gives the starting point (7:4–5; 11:1–2). In the book as a whole, Tamara Eskenazi argues, the repetition is deliberate: the same list frames the whole restoration, from the first return (Ezra 2) to the completion of the walls (Nehemiah 7), showing that the work of house, wall and law was done by one people across generations.

settings.what: Nehemiah puts Hanani and Hananiah in charge of Jerusalem
settings.to: Hanani, his brother, and Hananiah, commander of the fortress by the Temple
settings.when: After the wall and its doors were finished, autumn 445 (or 444) BC
settings.why: To leave the city in trusted hands: a brother, and a man chosen because he was faithful and feared God. With Nehemiah's enemies writing to Jerusalem's nobles (6:17–19), loyalty mattered more than rank.

settings.to: Hanani and Hananiah, and the gatekeepers and citizens who would keep watch
settings.when: After the wall and its doors were finished, autumn 445 (or 444) BC
settings.why: To keep a nearly empty city safe: gates opened late and shut while the guards were still on duty, and citizens posted near their own homes, where they had most reason to stay alert.

settings.what: The register of those who came back
settings.by: An older document, the "family register of those who had come up first" (7:5), copied by Nehemiah; the same list as Ezra 2
settings.to: Originally the community of Yehud and its leaders; here, Nehemiah and the assembly he gathered to be enrolled (7:5)
settings.when: Compiled from one or more returns between 538 and about 520 BC, or later; found and reused by Nehemiah in 445 (or 444) BC
settings.why: To show who belonged to the community, by family, town and clergy, as the basis for a new enrollment and for filling Jerusalem with people (11:1–2). Knowing that Nehemiah was planning to move families into the city explains why an old list matters at this point.
settings.readers: For the book's readers, the list tied their families to the first return and placed the walled city in the hands of the same people who had rebuilt the Temple.
views: Williamson and others: Ezra 2 was taken from this chapter.
Others: Nehemiah's editor took the list from Ezra.
Some: both drew on a Temple or provincial register.

settings.what: The governor's ruling on the unproven priests
settings.by: The governor (Tirshatha) of the list, probably Sheshbazzar or Zerubbabel; in Nehemiah's book the title also belongs to Nehemiah (8:9; 10:1)
settings.to: The priestly families of Hobaiah, Hakkoz and Barzillai, who had no family records
settings.when: Soon after a return, as in Ezra 2:63; the date depends on when the list itself was made
settings.why: To protect the holiness of the priesthood without a final judgment: they could not eat the most holy food until God answered by the Urim and Thummim. Repeated here, the ruling shows that Nehemiah's city kept the same standard of descent for its priests.
